Only partially, and the paper cannot settle our question — but our own repo already does.

WHAT SURVIVES. Every Table 1 number quoted is real. I checked all 50 cells against the LaTeX source, including the three MBPP AlphaCode-C cells the colleague added beyond what any summary gives (davinci-001 56.2, INCODER-6B 26.7, CODEGEN-MONO-16B 41.0). n=100 samples/task for HumanEval and MBPP, confirmed in the Table 1 caption and Appendix A. I also recomputed all 20 INFERRED gap-fraction values independently; every one matches to rounding. The arithmetic is clean.

WHERE IT DOES NOT TRANSFER.
(a) k. AlphaCode-C pass@1 selects 1 from a 100-sample pool. There is no k<=8 pool condition anywhere in the paper. Our regime is 3-4 draws now, 8 planned.
(b) The baseline is not one object. For the three Codex rows, baseline pass@1 is GREEDY, temperature 0, n=1 (3_experimental_setup.tex and Appendix A: "for baseline pass@1, we use the greedy search setting with temperature 0"), while AlphaCode-C and CodeT select from a temperature-0.8, n=100 pool. So "fraction of the pass@10 - pass@1 gap closed" mixes two decoding distributions on those rows and is not a selector-vs-selector comparison.
(c) The only two like-for-like rows are the two the colleague leans on, but for the wrong reason. For INCODER-6B and CODEGEN-MONO-16B the baseline pass@1 IS a selector over the same 100-pool (highest mean log-probability, temperature near 0). Those are the two cells where clustering nearly vanishes (+1.3 HumanEval, +5.4 MBPP) or goes negative (-2.4, -1.4). The cause is not "weak model," it is "the baseline there is already a competent reranker." That refinement makes the pessimistic reading STRONGER for us, because our incumbent (visible-assertion filter, 0.7455) is likewise already a real execution-based selector.
(d) Double-counting. Our 0.0737 is measured net of an execution filter (0.8192 oracle minus 0.7455 visible-picker). AlphaCode-C's gain is measured over a baseline with NO execution filtering, and MBR-exec's own ablation (44-expr-analysis.tex) states that "simply involving executability checking significantly helps improve the performance of all non-semantic feature-based selection methods." So scaling 21% onto our post-filter gap OVERSTATES the expected gain, it does not understate it.

THE COST ARGUMENT IS VOID for the variant we actually proposed. Pure cross-candidate execution agreement needs no expected outputs and no receiver calls at all — it reruns candidates already in the logs. Our own G1b run did 870 task-cells in 105.5 seconds of sandbox time, zero receiver calls. The 909-calls/hour budget is only binding against full CodeT (model-written tests), not against the plan under review.

  code-davinci-001: baseline pass@1 34.8 (-4.2) | CodeT pass@1 60.4 (+10.2)

CodeT pass@1 goes UP by +9.0 to +14.1 absolute when the example assertions are left visible. CodeT's margin over baseline is LARGER with a visible assertion: +26.9 / +25.6 / +27.2, versus +11.0 / +11.2 / +18.8 on the stripped contexts. The paper's own sentence: "the performance of CodeT is significantly improved using the original benchmark." Assertions were removed to stop CodeT being INFLATED by leaked ground truth, not because visibility hurts it. So "the single published measurement of this method family in a regime with a visible example assertion is a negative number" is the exact opposite of what the paper reports. For us this flips sign: one visible assertion is a FAVORABLE condition for execution-based selection, not a handicap.

2. TABLE 4 IS CHERRY-PICKED, and the cherry-picking reverses the cost conclusion. 56.5 is real, but it is the single worst cell: Limit=1, Sampling Number=10. Full pass@1 65.8 is Limit=5, SN=100. The same 4x5 grid (code-davinci-002, HumanEval) reads:
  Limit=1: 56.5 / 57.5 / 60.7 / 62.4   (SN = 10 / 20 / 50 / 100)
  Limit=2: 62.2 / 62.8 / 63.2 / 63.6
  Limit=3: 62.9 / 63.2 / 65.5 / 65.0
  Limit=4: 64.1 / 64.5 / 65.7 / 65.0
  Limit=5: 63.9 / 64.2 / 65.2 / 65.8
Sampling Number IS the receiver-call axis. At SN=10, Limit=4 the score is 64.1 — 97% of full CodeT for one tenth of the test-generation calls. The paper's claim is exactly this: "CodeT improves the pass@1 by 9.5% with only 10 test cases... suggesting the high test case efficiency. We can use a smaller Sampling Number in real-world application to balance the performance and computation cost." The colleague's paraphrase drops the paper's conjunction — the actual text is that the gap narrows when "Sampling Number >= 50 AND Limit >= 3" — and thereby converts an efficiency result into a cost objection.

Not REFUTED: the paper exists at the stated id, every Table 1 cell is verbatim correct at the stated k, model and benchmark, n=100 is right, the Table 4 value 56.5 is real, the ~381-411 test-case counts are real, and all 20 derived gap fractions recompute exactly. The colleague read the paper.

The Table 4 claim quotes the worst cell of a 4x5 grid whose actual purpose is to show that the receiver-call axis (Sampling Number) can be cut 10x for a 1.7-point loss — turning the paper's efficiency result into a cost objection it does not support.

The colleague's BOTTOM LINE — that cross-candidate execution agreement will not recover our selection gap and that any effect is at the edge of measurability on our budget — is correct, and is now measured directly on our own receivers rather than transferred. But it is correct at 0-6.5% of gap for agreement alone, not 21%, and for a reason the colleague did not identify: mean cluster count 1.63 / 1.28 at 3-4 draws. applies_to_our_regime:
LARGELY NO. Every quoted number is real; the three decision-relevant conclusions do not transfer. Four independent regime breaks:

(1) k. Paper: N=50 (N=100 for the Table 1 ablation). Us: k<=8. The paper does NOT study small N — NOT FOUND, no N-sensitivity sweep exists (the only sweep is over D, the input count). Table 6 diagnostics: 1.20-1.43 behavioral clusters per problem, largest cluster 47.2-48.5 of 50. Their clustering is near-DEGENERATE: ~94% of candidates share one fingerprint. At k=8 the same structure gives a largest cluster of ~7-8/8 and no discriminative signal; a fragmented pool gives 2-vs-1 pluralities that are sampling noise. The paper's own failure analysis says so directly (Section 5.4): failed problems have "an average largest-cluster size of 25.6 (versus 38-48 in the typical case)" — clustering fails precisely when clusters are fragmented, which is our expected regime.

(2) Model strength. Closed-weight Gemini only. The paper's WEAKEST model (Flash Lite) scores 91.0-91.8 on MBPP+ and 90.9-93.3 on HumanEval+, with oracle 93.9-99%. We run q4_k_m Qwen2.5-3B at 0.7169 single-attempt / 0.8192 oracle pass@3, and our informative band (230 tasks) is lower still. Limitations section: "We evaluate Gemini models on two Python benchmarks; other model families or languages require new runs." No statement anywhere about small, weak, open-weight or quantized models — NOT FOUND. Plurality consensus assumes the modal behavior is correct; that assumption is untested below ~90% per-candidate accuracy, and in our informative band it is likely violated (correlated failure modes cluster together, so the largest cluster can be actively anti-correlated with correctness).

(3) Inputs. Their dominant lever requires an LLM to generate D=50 inputs per problem (an extra call: ~500 in + 500 out tokens, Appendix B). We have ONE visible assertion. Their D-sweep bottoms out at D=5; D=1-3 is never measured — NOT FOUND.

(4) Baseline mismatch, and this one is decisive. Their "Best-of-N" is "first syntactically valid candidate" from a pool already stripped of invalid generations — i.e. essentially a RANDOM valid candidate, roughly equal to single-sample accuracy. Our cheap filter is "first candidate whose visible assertion passes" (0.7455 vs 0.7169 single attempt) — an execution-grounded filter using a real expected output. The paper's "clustering does not beat the cheap filter" is therefore "clustering does not beat random" and sets a MUCH weaker bar than ours. Relatedly, the colleague mismaps our regime onto their EXAMPLE-ONLY row: their example-only strategy uses example INPUTS only, with no expected outputs, purely as clustering probes. Our one MBPP assertion carries an expected output, so we sit in a cell the paper never tests — better-informed on the filter, worse-off on distinguishing inputs.

CEILING ARTIFACT (the core misapplication). The paper's own stated reason for its headline null is a ceiling, not a law: "with selection-failure rates already at 1.5-2.7%, the residual room for any aggregator to differentiate is small." Their entire oracle gap is 2.8% (HumanEval+) / 3.9% (MBPP+). Our selection gap is 7.37pp on the 3B — larger than their whole generation-plus-selection gap. Nothing measured inside a 2.4pp window bounds behavior inside a 7.4pp window.

STATISTICAL POWER. Appendix C, Table 7 (HumanEval+, 164 problems): the 95% CIs are ±1.83 to ±3.05pp (e.g. Flash low SV-WV = -0.61 [-3.05, +1.22], p=0.394). "Statistically indistinguishable" here is absence of evidence from an underpowered test, not evidence of equivalence — a true 1-2pp aggregation-rule effect would be undetectable. MBPP+ (375-378 problems) is tighter (~±1pp) but still cannot exclude ~1pp. A 1pp effect matters to us.

DIRECTION OF THE PAPER'S OWN DIVERSITY RESULT. Section 5.2: deeper thinking improves output-pattern MV by ~12pp while "execution-based methods stay flat or decrease slightly" because "deeper thinking appears to reduce candidate diversity, leaving fewer distinct behavioral clusters to exploit." The paper thus establishes that exec-based selection NEEDS diversity and degrades as diversity falls — it only ever probes the low-diversity end. Our regime (weak quantized model, temperature sampling) is the untested high-diversity end, where the sign of the effect is unknown in both directions.

WHAT DOES TRANSFER: (a) output-pattern majority voting is comprehensively dominated — 19-52pp below the best exec-based selector on every configuration, and consistently below even Best-of-N; "MV never solves a problem that any execution-based method misses" (Appendix B). Do not build the naive-string-MV arm. The stated cause is the all-or-nothing filter: when every candidate errors on some generated input, MV returns nothing. Keep exception-aware fingerprints if we cluster at all. (b) AST-normalized MV recovers 20-40pp of that but leaves a 1.8-3.1pp residual (Table 3) — cheap, worth having, not sufficient. (c) Input source dominates aggregation rule. (d) Section 5.4: "greedy decoding rescues 88 of the 119 errors" SemanticVote makes — a temperature-0 draw is a cheap, complementary prior/tie-break and is arguably a better use of budget than more clustering inputs. This is an untested, cheap, pro-project arm the colleague did not extract.

Discount for k=8 (statistical power of a plurality vote scales with pool size; at k=8 the modal cluster is decided by 1-2 candidates), for D=1 (below the paper's smallest tested D=5), and for a 3B vs Flash Lite (~20pp weaker). Realistic ceiling in the example-only configuration: +0.5pp, and that is generous.
- Central estimate: 0.0pp. Directly anchored on the Lite low example-only cell, where all three aggregators equal Best-of-N exactly. Our baseline (visible-assertion filter, 0.7455) is strictly stronger than the paper's baseline, which pushes the estimate further toward or below zero.
- Downside: plausibly -1 to -3pp, and the paper cannot bound this. Our informative band (230 tasks) is selected for difficulty, so per-candidate accuracy there is well below 0.5. Largest-cluster selection with correlated failure modes (a shared off-by-one, a shared misreading of the spec) will systematically return the wrong answer, and it can override a candidate that our single visible assertion already certified. The paper's own mechanism note supports this: failures concentrate where the largest cluster is small (25.6/50), which is exactly our expected cluster geometry, and "the correct solution exists but is not the plurality behavior in the sampled pool."

But to approach the paper's regime you need D>=5-10 diverse inputs, and at that point you are trading draws for probes. With k fixed at 8, spending 1-2 draws' worth of budget on input generation reduces the oracle ceiling you are selecting from — and Table 5's decomposition says generation failure (3.9%) already exceeds selection failure (2.7%) even in their favorable regime. In our numbers the oracle ceiling is 0.8192 at 3 draws, so draws buy headroom directly and measurably.

RECOMMENDATION FOR THE DECISION. Do NOT collapse the aggregation branch on the strength of this paper — its equivalence result is an underpowered null (CIs ±1.8-3.0pp) measured under a 2.4pp ceiling with near-degenerate clusters (1.2-1.4 clusters/problem), and at k=8 tie-breaking rules matter MORE, not less, than at k=50. Also do NOT run the execution-agreement arm as a naive largest-cluster vote on the single visible assertion's input: that is the paper's Lite/example-only cell, which measures as exactly zero gain over the cheapest filter, and it is the one configuration we can already predict. The defensible cheap experiment, if the arm is run at all, is: (a) exception-aware fingerprints, never output-pattern MV (19-52pp penalty, robustly measured); (b) one extra receiver call per task to generate 5-10 diverse inputs, since D=5 already captures most of the paper's D-scaling gain (95.1 of 97.0); (c) a temperature-0 greedy draw as prior and tie-break, since greedy rescued 88 of 119 SemanticVote errors in the paper and it costs one call; (d) cluster agreement layered ON TOP of the visible-assertion filter, not instead of it, with the 0.7455 filter as the baseline to beat. Scope it as a ~2-3 hour pilot on the 230-task informative band and pre-register a stop rule: if cluster-based selection does not beat 0.7455 with a CI excluding zero on the band, the execution-agreement branch is dead and the remaining viability question moves to STOPPING rather than selection.

expected_gain_in_our_regime:
LARGELY UNKNOWN, AND THE HONEST PRIOR IS ZERO. The paper's own internals bound the expectation downward on four independent counts; none of them is an extrapolation of a published number, which is why I will not manufacture a point estimate.

The one defensible anchor: the tier we could conceivably afford is the no_mem tier, and INFERRED that tier recovers 40.1% of gap on HumanEval versus CodeT's 41.2% -- i.e. no measurable gain over methods that already exist. And we cannot even reach that tier: no_mem still needs 5 GPT-4o-generated common inputs plus LLM equivalence refinement, and CodeT needs Codex-generated test cases. Our achievable tier is strictly BELOW no_mem/CodeT.

Four downward pressures specific to us:
1. ORACLE ACCURACY. The membership component carries ~24.6pp and requires an oracle at p > 0.5; o1-mini measures only p = 0.61-0.72, and the paper's own bound needs p >= 0.9 with n >= 25 for P(A) >= 0.89. A quantized 3B sits at ~0.5, where the Copeland tournament is uninformative. This component is simply unavailable to us.
2. CLUSTER COUNT AT k = 8. With 8 candidates and a handful of inputs, expect 2-4 distinct output clusters. Copeland has essentially no redundancy to average oracle noise over, and ties between equal-size clusters (2 vs 2, 3 vs 3) are frequent, so "largest cluster" degenerates to a coin flip on precisely the tasks where selection matters. The paper's k-dependence statement points the same way.
3. ONE VISIBLE ASSERTION. Clustering needs COMMON inputs. With exactly one visible input, output clustering collapses to a binary agrees/does-not-agree partition -- which is information our 0.7455 baseline already consumes in full. To get more inputs we must have the 3B write them; a quantized 3B's MBPP inputs will often be type-invalid and crash all candidates, yielding degenerate all-one-cluster or all-singleton partitions. That is a NEW failure mode absent from the paper, where GPT-4o wrote the inputs.
4. HEADROOM AND DETECTABILITY. Total headroom is 0.0737 (3B). Even a generous 30%-of-gap recovery is +2.2pp. INFERRED power sketch at n = 448 for a paired binary comparison: SE of the paired difference is sqrt(d/448) for discordance rate d, so a +2pp effect is 1.89 SE at d = 0.05, 1.34 SE at d = 0.10, 1.09 SE at d = 0.15. A realistic effect would NOT clear significance on our current n. Contrast with the effects we HAVE detected (adaptive best-of-N vs feedback loop: -0.0182, CI [-0.0260, -0.0105]) -- those are the magnitudes our design can resolve.

COST, for the record, is NOT the obstacle. Reusing the k=8 draws plus ~5 self-generated inputs per task is roughly 561-1100 extra receiver calls, about 0.6-1.2 contended hours -- trivially affordable. So if we run execution-agreement clustering, run it as a cheap, pre-registered, negative-result-tolerant check with the null as the stated expectation, not as a rescue. This paper supplies no grounds for expecting it to close the 0.0737.

YES on the four axes that usually break a citation, and this is unusually well matched — but with three real boundary gaps, one of which the colleague has the sign wrong on.

MATCHES (all MEASURED-IN-PAPER):
1. k. Primary and external pools are k=8 at T=0.8. This is OUR planned k, not the k=50-1000 of most selection work. No large-k dependence.
2. Baseline. BoN is defined as "return the first public-passer in pool order", i* = min{i: pass(c_i, T_pub)=1}. That is LITERALLY our 0.7455 baseline's estimator form ("return the first candidate whose visible assertion passes"). This is the single most important match and it holds exactly.
3. Method. "Consensus" is MBR-Exec: among public-passers, take the per-probe plurality fingerprint and select the candidate of greatest agreement, tie-broken by embedding medoid. Fingerprints come from a deterministic probe bank Pi(t) of at most 24 inputs (public-test arguments plus type-aware mutations), coordinates in {repr[:200], ERR:<type>, NOFUNC, NOCODE, TIMEOUT}. This IS cross-candidate execution agreement — our exact untested candidate.
4. No confounds we were worried about. No model-written tests (probe bank is mutations of public args, not LLM-generated inputs). Models are WEAKER than ours (0.5-1.5B vs 3B/7B), so the negative cannot be dismissed as "strong model, no headroom". Hidden-test oracle, leakage-free by construction, matched compute.
5. Benchmarks. HumanEval+ (n=164) and MBPP+ (n=370, after a determinism gate drops 8/378). MBPP+ is built on MBPP-sanitized, which is our split.

GAPS (in decreasing honesty of the colleague's framing):
(a) VISIBLE-FILTER STRENGTH — REAL, AND THE QUOTED PREDICTION IS REAL, BUT ITS SIGN IS NOT ONE-DIRECTIONAL. Verbatim from the paper: "a weaker visible-test filter (so that visible-passing, hidden-wrong majorities become common) would refill the consensus trap, and a genuinely coverage-increasing intervention ... would move the wall. Operators that re-rank what is already there cannot." Our one-assertion MBPP split is that weaker filter. The colleague is right that this is a prediction, not a measurement, and flags it honestly. BUT: the probe bank is built FROM the public tests ("public-test arguments plus type-aware mutations"). Weakening the visible filter to ONE assertion simultaneously (i) refills the trap and (ii) starves the fingerprint down to one seed argument plus mutations. Semantic Voting (arXiv:2605.08680) measures that input quality is the dominant factor, not the aggregation rule: sketch-based input generation beats direct LLM generation by 0.6-2.1 pp and beats random fuzzing by up to 11.3 pp, while SemanticVote, weighted voting and MBR-Exec are "statistically indistinguishable across all 18 configurations". So gap (a) cuts both ways and the report presents only the favorable half.
(b) NO 3B/7B CELL — REAL. Paper explicitly bounds itself: "the model axis covers the 0.5-1.5B range across two families". It makes no extrapolation to larger scale. But see corrected_numbers: the colleague's 4.3-4.6pp vs 7.37pp bridge is not like-for-like and conflates headroom with trap mass.

Their own k=16 probe puts 16/30 hard tasks in the coverage bucket. PARTLY UNKNOWN, AND THE UNKNOWN PART IS IRREDUCIBLE FROM THE LITERATURE — no paper measures execution agreement at k<=8 on a quantized 3B behind a one-assertion filter. What can be bounded:

DECOMPOSITION (the paper's, and it is sound). Net gain = P(visible-surviving plurality is hidden-wrong AND a hidden-correct candidate is in the pool AND the fingerprint plurality selects it) - P(BoN was already right AND consensus moves off it). The second term is not negligible: with a one-assertion filter, many survivors are hidden-wrong, so consensus can actively migrate off a correct first-passer. Their b10 was 0-1 per cell only because their full-suite filter had already removed most wrong candidates before consensus ran. Ours will not. EXPECT NONZERO HARM in our regime — this is a downside the report does not mention at all.

ANCHORS: paper captures 14.0% of headroom pooled at k=8 on 0.5-1.5B with a STRONG filter (+1 to +3 tasks per cell, i.e. +0.3 to +0.8pp absolute). DOCE gets +1.6pp on top of filtering at n=50 on an unquantized 7B and says there is "little space" above that.

FORCES IN OUR FAVOUR: (1) our BoN is weak (+2.86pp from the visible assertion vs DOCE's +22.4pp from full filtering), so the bar is low and the plurality is being compared against something near a random survivor pick — strongest argument, and it is structural, not hopeful; (2) the paper's own quoted refill prediction; (3) q4_k_m on a 3B gives HIGH candidate diversity, and Semantic Voting finds execution-based methods "stay flat or degrade as candidate diversity falls" — we are at the favourable end of that axis.
FORCES AGAINST: (1) thin probe bank — one seed argument plus type-aware mutations vs their up-to-24 from a full public suite, against a measured finding that input quality dominates (up to 11.3pp penalty for poor inputs); (2) coverage wall — oracle pass@3 = 0.8192 means ~18% of tasks are unreachable by ANY selector, and their k=16 probe found 16/30 hard tasks still uncovered; (3) plurality over <=8 candidates is frequently a cluster of size 2-3, a high-variance estimator; (4) nonzero b10 from the weak filter, as above.

HONEST POINT FORECAST on the 3B: +0 to +2.5pp, most plausibly +0.5 to +1.5pp, i.e. 10-25% of the selection gap — squarely consistent with the paper's 14% and DOCE's +1.6pp at 6x budget. On the 7B (gap 0.0351) expect proportionally less, likely indistinguishable from zero.

THE DECISIVE CONSTRAINT IS POWER, NOT EFFECT SIGN. The paper could not reach significance at +1 to +3 tasks with 164-370 tasks per cell. Our informative band is 230 tasks — FEWER. A +1pp effect on 230 tasks is ~2 tasks; paired McNemar on that is hopeless. So: even if execution agreement works exactly as well as the best published evidence allows, WE CANNOT DEMONSTRATE IT SIGNIFICANTLY on 230 tasks at k=8. Any plan whose success criterion is "significant recovery of the gap" is underpowered before it starts and should be rejected on those grounds alone, independent of the paper.

COMPUTE: 230 tasks x 8 draws x 2 receivers = 3,680 receiver calls, plus execution of ~24 probes per candidate (cheap, local). At 909 calls/hour that is ~4 contended hours — well inside budget. So the experiment is CHEAP; the problem is that it is not DECISIVE.

RECOMMENDATION. Do not run it as a confirmatory gap-recovery experiment. Run it as a one-shot MEASUREMENT of the paper's own mechanism variables on our data, which is what our regime can actually resolve: (i) measure our trap mass directly — count tasks where the one-assertion-surviving plurality is hidden-wrong AND a hidden-correct candidate is in the pool. That single count tests the paper's refill prediction against our weaker filter and is the whole question. If it is near zero, the project's selection half is dead and we have replicated the paper in the regime it predicted would differ. (ii) Measure the hidden-correctness AUC of execution-agreement features among visible-passers and compare against their 0.479 — this is the behavioural test that neither their scissors probe nor our static GBM/logistic audit performed, and it is the only genuinely new evidence available to us. (iii) Take ACE as the ready-made baseline for the stopping half and adopt Proposition 1's n>=45 as a design constraint; our 230-task band clears it. The stopping half is where our numbers can actually support a claim.

Quantized small models have strongly correlated errors (same off-by-one, same misreading of an ambiguous spec, same empty-input handling), so wrong answers cluster as tightly as right ones. Clustering then amplifies the modal error rather than correcting it. Their 3B started from an 18.4% pass rate against a no-filter random pick; the plurality only had to beat random. We need it to beat an already-informative filter on a pre-filtered adversarial subset.

The measured gain on top of visible filtering is +0.0095 (3B) and +0.0044 (7B), both ~12.5% of the respective gaps, both with intervals covering zero. Claim (2) does not survive: DOCE does not show our selection gap is recoverable at our k, and our own G1b audit shows it largely is not. The gap should be treated as mostly unrecoverable by cheap hidden-test-blind selection at k<=8, with one cheap zero-receiver-call ablation (probe count 8 -> 20-30) owed to DOCE's Figure 4 before the line is closed.

Reading 2, fraction-of-gap transfer, which I consider the more defensible one. Their k=8 baselines sit 28-64% absolute with pass@8 oracles that are certainly tens of pp higher (unmeasured -- this step is an assumption, not a paper number). If their k=8 gap is 25-35pp, the cluster-size increment is 11-25% of the available gap. Applied to our 7.37pp gap that is +0.8 to +1.8pp on the 3B, and under +0.9pp on the 7B whose gap is only 3.51pp. Table 7 (Claude 3 Opus, Random 78.03 / SRank 79.18) is the paper's one datapoint at an absolute level near ours and it lands at +1.15pp, consistent with this reading.

Further discounts specific to us, none of them quantified by the paper: (a) the paper's own floor is >=30 test inputs and warns that below that the combined score can go negative; we have 1 visible assertion and would be self-generating inputs from a quantized 3B that will emit duplicates and crashers; (b) MBPP-sanitized functions mostly return small scalars, so output-agreement collapses to few distinct outputs, producing degenerate near-universal clusters and frequent ties -- with k<=8 cluster sizes are integers 1..8, a granularity the paper never studies (its smallest reported k is 2 but on 100-solution-trained intuitions); (c) P(both wrong | agree) is 0.37 for the paper's weakest model and plausibly worse for ours, so the failure mode is a confident-wrong plurality, which is exactly the mode that a 909-call budget cannot afford to discover late; (d) the paper's crossover means our existing 3-4 draw logs are below the k where plain largest-cluster even beats a single sample -- do not test this on the existing logs.
One discount runs the other way: our visible-assertion filter already removes crashers, so we would be operating in the ClusterSize+PassRate regime (the stronger line) rather than ClusterSize alone.

BOTTOM LINE for the decision: expect +1 to +3pp over the 0.7455 baseline on the 3B, centered near +1.5pp, with a real probability mass on zero and a small mass on negative; expect essentially nothing measurable on the 7B. That is still strictly better than the static-feature models, which recovered fractions -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00 with all intervals covering zero, so ONE pre-registered experiment is warranted. Design it as: k=8, the 230-task informative band, primary contrast = largest-output-agreement-cluster-among-visible-assertion-survivors versus visible-assertion-first, tie-break pre-registered (e.g. lowest index, or shortest candidate), plus a fresh oracle pass@8 measured on the same pool so a fraction-of-gap is computable this time. Cost about 2,070 receiver calls, ~2.3 contended hours, not 22. Do NOT build the learned inter-cluster scorer: its measured margin over plain largest-cluster is -1.97 to +5.03pp on MBPP-S at N=100, it needs pass-rate features that require CORRECT expected outputs we do not have, and at k<=8 the interaction matrix is 8x8 at most.

CodeT's own paper (arXiv:2207.10397) says its clustering-only baseline AlphaCode-C "is consistently inferior to CodeT ... demonstrating the superiority of our dual execution agreement that takes test case information into consideration."

Forces pushing UP: weaker policy models show the largest selection gains in both papers (InCoder-6B +5.4 from pure clustering; Llama3-8B is where every delta is largest), and our 3B has the larger gap of the two receivers.

My honest expectation, INFERRED and low-confidence: on the 230-task informative band with a 3B at k=8, clustering on the single visible input, somewhere in [-0.01, +0.02] with a CI that will cover zero at this sample size. With synthesized input diversity but NO synthesized expected outputs -- the AlphaCode-C recipe, the only version of CodeT's advantage we can actually afford -- perhaps [0.00, +0.035], still likely CI-covering-zero on 230 tasks. I would not bet on recovering more than half of the 0.0737.

Power reality, which should drive the decision more than any point estimate. Detecting a true +0.02 paired effect on 230 tasks is marginal; our own successful comparisons landed effects like -0.0182 with CI [-0.0260, -0.0105], so we can resolve roughly 0.018-0.026 with paired designs at this n. If the true effect is under ~0.02 we will not distinguish it from zero, and at 909 calls/hour an 8-draw run over 230 tasks is ~1840 receiver calls (~2 contended hours) plus clustering execution -- cheap enough to be worth one pilot, and cheap enough that a null result is affordable information rather than a sunk arm.

Recommended framing: run the pilot, but pre-register it as a bounded test against the 0.0737 ceiling, not against this paper's deltas. Build the synthesized-input / no-synthesized-output variant (AlphaCode-C recipe), since the expected-output ingredient that produces CodeT's +10.00 requires a generator stronger than our receivers and is out of reach on an M5 with no API budget.
